description: We are the Espace Odyssey Team. We are a motivated group of AI Master's students interested in applying AI and Machine Learning to solve challenges related to Earth and Space exploration.
summary: Moon Twins on Earth is an open method and web app that finds the places on Earth closest to a planned lunar base site, and shows why. Earth analog sites are usually picked by eye; we measure them. The same code reads NASA lunar elevation and illumination data (Shackleton crater, two craters in Artemis III candidate regions, and the lunar maria) and Earth elevation data on one 60 m grid, turning every difference into a 0–100 % similarity. In one night it searched about 265,000 cells and ranked 1,261 dry, crater-like places, finding real impact craters from elevation alone. In the app, anyone can explore the ranking on two linked globes, open a card for each site (what matches, where the analogy breaks down, how to get there) and fly into the 3D terrain. It is made for people to learn what makes a good base site and to discover new places beyond the famous analog sites. Our main contribution is the method: repeatable, open, and built to scale to the whole planet and new lunar targets.
details:
Moon Twins on Earth is an open, reusable pipeline that measures how Moon-like a place on Earth is and ranks the best Earth stand-ins ("twins") for candidate lunar base sites. Analog sites have mostly been chosen by eye. Our method can be rerun and extended: for any lunar site, it finds the places on Earth that come closest, shows how close they are, and says where the comparison breaks down. Our ranking and our web app are the first results built on it; we want the pipeline itself to be the base that others build on.

What it does and how it works

The pipeline: one ruler for two worlds

  1. Moon target. The lunar site is measured from NASA data with the same code used for Earth. For Shackleton crater, the pipeline finds the bowl in NASA's 20 m LOLA south-pole elevation map: 20.9 km wide, about 4.1 km deep, inner walls 27.2°. NASA PGDA illumination maps give the sunlit rim and the permanently dark floor. SLDEM2015 (LOLA + JAXA Kaguya) gives the mare plains.
  2. Earth search. Any region, or the whole land surface, is split into cells of about 15 km, the size of an Artemis III landing region. ESA WorldCover removes forest, cropland, water, wetlands and towns (with a 2 km buffer). The Copernicus 30 m elevation model is reprojected to the same 60 m metric grid as the Moon. All data streams directly from AWS Open Data, with no manual downloads.
  3. Measure. Each criterion is one function, applied the same way to Earth and Moon: bowl shape, steep walls, a flat landing pad, roughness, drivable ground, and light (sunny ridge, dark floor, light next to dark). On Earth, light comes from simulating a full year of Sun over the terrain. Raw values are stored.
  4. Score. Each criterion becomes a similarity, exp(−((Earth − Moon) / tolerance)²), where 1 means identical to the Moon; the total is a weighted mean. Because scoring is a separate step, a new lunar target is scored against every Earth place already measured, without recomputing the terrain.
  5. Filter. Post-filters remove known false matches: open-pit mines (global mining polygons) and icy, wet or vegetated bowls. A filter never changes a score.
  6. Export. Plain CSV and JSON files in a documented format, read by our app and by any other tool.

Built to be reused

  • New region: one command with a bounding box (run_pipeline.py --bbox W S E N). The world search runs overnight on one laptop and picks up where it stopped.
  • New lunar site: add its measured values to a config file; the next export scores every Earth place against it. That is how we added two smaller craters in Artemis III regions (de Gerlache rim, Haworth) and four individual maria next to Shackleton and the mare median.
  • New criterion: add one function and a weight. Our criteria document lists 29 criteria; the app shows a criterion as soon as the export has data for it.
  • Settings (thresholds, weights, tolerances) live in config files, not in the code. They are frozen with git tags and guarded by automated tests, so a change shows up as a new version instead of silently changing results.
  • Mars is the natural next step: the Earth side stays as it is; a Mars target needs a reader for Mars elevation data and Mars-specific criteria.

What we built on it in 48 hours

  • The search: about 265,000 cells (11,604 of 19,433 one-degree land tiles, deserts first); 1,825 crater-like places scored.
  • Real craters from elevation alone: Meteor Crater, Roter Kamm and Pingualuit, which it was never told about.
  • Mines and ice: it also found 111 open-pit mines, such as Chuquicamata and Escondida. After the mine and dry-bowl filters, 1,261 places are ranked.
  • Top results: #1 is a bowl in the Tian Shan, China, 60 % similar to Shackleton, with walls as steep (27.3° vs 27.2°). Meteor Crater, a known training site, ranks 10th (46 %).
  • Shape twins are not light twins: no place ranks high on both.
  • Earth has no grazing Sun: at Shackleton the Sun never rises above 1.9°; on Earth it reaches at least 23.4°.
  • Mare: flat ground like the Moon's is common on Earth, but small craters and basalt are rare.
  • A live web app with two linked 3D globes. Pick a base on the Moon and the Earth turns to its best twins. Each site has a card with a radar chart, Earth and Moon values side by side, what matches and what is missing, ground conditions, access (nearest city, airport and research station) and a 3D close-up with the crater outlined and a lunar base drawn to scale.

Benefits

  • Choosing an analog site becomes a measured comparison, criterion by criterion, that anyone can check and rerun. Every score traces back to a raw value next to the Moon value.
  • Teams can pick a field site for what they want to test (steep-wall traverses, landing pads, rough terrain, shadowed floors), see how to reach it, and see clearly what Earth cannot rehearse.
  • It looks beyond the well-known sites: apart from Meteor Crater, our top 10 are remote bowls in Central Asia, Turkey, the Sahara, the Danakil and the Andes.

Intended impact

  • Give analog-campaign, rover and instrument teams a ranked shortlist of field sites for each lunar site, with the limits stated.
  • Help people learn what makes a good lunar base site and discover new places on Earth themselves: the app explains every step in plain words and runs in any browser, for students, teachers and the public.
  • Be a shared, open base: others can plug in new Artemis candidate sites as they are announced, new criteria, or new planets.

How it is creative

  • The lunar target is measured, not looked up: from NASA data, with the same code and on the same grid as every Earth cell, so the comparison is fair by construction.
  • Every Earth place gets a "closest lunar twin" among several real lunar sites.
  • Sunlight is a measured criterion: simulated over Earth craters and compared with the lunar pole's illumination.
  • We show failures on purpose: known sites the method missed are listed, with the reason.

Factors we considered

  • Scale: Shackleton is 21 km wide and most Earth bowls are far smaller, so we compare shape, not size.
  • Resolution: slope and roughness depend on grid size, so both worlds use one 60 m metric grid.
  • Honest validation: we froze the settings before testing on held-out sites. We missed Haughton (too eroded), Askja (its lake leaves the caldera only 48 m deep, under our 50 m minimum), Tenoumer (44 m) and Lanzarote (sea and villages fail the filter). The app shows these misses.
  • Missing data shows as "no data", never as zero; in our export every ranked place has a value for every counted criterion.
  • Known limits: lunar light maps measure the Sun's disc, our Earth simulation its centre. Earth cannot reproduce low gravity, vacuum, radiation or the mare's day–night temperature swing.
  • No machine learning: no labelled list of good analogs exists, and physical measurements keep every score traceable.
  • Open licences only, so anyone can reuse the whole stack.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Python: NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj, GeoPandas, pandas, PyYAML, pystac-client, Matplotlib, Plotly, pytest.
  • Web: JavaScript, HTML and CSS with globe.gl and MapLibre GL JS; hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • Data access: read directly from AWS Open Data, NASA PGDA, PANGAEA and the Macrostrat API. Git and GitHub.
  • Hardware: our own laptops.
  • Claude Code as a coding assistant (details in the SI field).
